subject_entity.notes: Montanist prophetess and one of the founding triad of the New Prophecy alongside Montanus and Priscilla. Active in Phrygia c. 155–179. Her prophecies were recorded and cited by both Montanist supporters and anti-Montanist critics in Eusebius HE 5.

object_entity.proposition_label: Prophetic Gifts Continue After the Apostles
object_entity.description: The Holy Spirit continues to give direct prophecy and ecstatic spiritual gifts beyond the apostolic age; new prophetic revelation may supplement or correct the established tradition. Affirmed by Montanists; opposed by the emerging episcopal mainstream who grounded authority in apostolic succession.

evidence.notes: Maximilla explicitly claims 'I am word, spirit, and power' — central Montanist prophetic claim.

passage.excerpt: Maximilla, likewise, said: 'I am driven from among the sheep like a wolf; I am no wolf — I am word, spirit, and power.' These prophecies of Montanus and Maximilla were opposed by those who took their stand on the tradition of the apostles. The anti-Montanist writer notes that he himself saw Maximilla's prophecies fail: she predicted wars and confusion, but peace followed after her death.

object_entity.notes: Founder of Montanism (the 'New Prophecy') in Phrygia c. 155–180. Claimed to speak as the Paraclete in the first person. Associated with prophetesses Maximilla and Priscilla (Prisca). Montanism taught rigorous fasting, the imminent New Jerusalem descending at Pepuza, and the continuation of ecstatic prophecy — generating controversy with emerging episcopal authority.

passage.excerpt: At this time in Phrygia, Montanus, as he was called, together with Alcibiades and Theodotus, gave the adversary occasion to suppose that he was the Paraclete. He was seized with frenzy and began to babble and utter strange sounds, prophesying contrary to the established custom of the Church handed down from the beginning. Of those who listened to this spurious utterance, some were vexed and rebuked him as one that was possessed and controlled by a demon — but others were elated, thinking this was the gift of the Spirit.

subject_entity.notes: Bishop of Corinth c. 166–174. Prolific letter-writer whose correspondence with churches in Athens, Sparta, Nicomedia, Gortyna (Crete), Amastris (Pontus), and Rome is recorded by Eusebius (HE 4.23). A key witness to the network of apostolic churches in the 2nd century and the authority of Peter and Paul at Rome and Corinth.

object_entity.proposition_label: Faith is transmitted through apostolic succession
object_entity.description: The bishops who succeed the apostles are authoritative guarantors of the received tradition.

evidence.notes: Dionysius affirms Peter and Paul jointly founded Corinth and Rome — apostolic double foundation.

passage.excerpt: In the same epistle Dionysius speaks of Paul and Peter: 'Both of them planted in our Corinth and taught us jointly. Having taught together in Italy, they suffered martyrdom at the same time.' This same Dionysius also wrote to the Athenians a letter of admonition, almost bringing them back to the faith, which they had abandoned as if after the martyrdom of Publius their bishop.
